prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials in this search yet, and the starting network scored 0 on both seeds. In earlier searches, only one network family ever scored above 0: about 0.22, with both seeds succeeding, on two different recipes. It feeds the legal-action mask in as per-type input channels under several layouts and maps per-type output channels back through the same layouts. Uniform zeros elsewhere suggest each world's actions or footprints may be arranged differently from its description. Recipe changes alone never helped. Round 1 should first confirm that this family works in this world (candidate 1). Candidate 2 tests whether covering all eight rotations and flips, instead of four layouts, catches more ways a world can deviate. Candidate 3 tests whether about 85% more training samples (fewer PPO epochs) lift the score. I will treat nonzero late-training success as the first real signal. A gap below about 0.05 between candidates is within seed noise.

### Round 2
The mask-layout family is the only one that has ever scored, but here it is barely above zero. With 4 or 8 layouts it scored 0.001 dev, with one seed at 0.002 and late training success of 0.001 to 0.002. With 2 PPO epochs it scored 0. All of these gaps are within seed noise. Since 8 layouts did no better than 4, an unhandled flip or transpose of the action layout is probably not the bottleneck. More likely, the agent cannot judge each placement precisely enough: where the brick lands under its footprint and whether every covered cell is a missing target cell. On 8x8x6 targets made of up to 16 bricks, an exact build needs nearly every step to be right. This round tests three things: a head that pools over the footprint without assuming its shape or anchor corner, global context fed into the trunk, and a recipe that reuses each sample more.

### Round 3
Only the 4-layout mask family shows any signal, and it grows with optimisation per sample: 0.000 at 2 PPO epochs, 0.001 at 4 and 0.0146 at 8 (r2c3, both seeds above 0). Late training success follows the same order (0 / 0.001 / 0.012). So this world seems limited by how much the network learns from few samples, not by what it can represent. 8 layouts matched 4 layouts at 4 epochs, so a missing dihedral layout is unlikely to be the cause. r2c1 (footprint pooling) and r2c2 (global context) scored 0 at 4 epochs, but the baseline only scored 0.001 there, so that recipe cannot tell networks apart and neither idea is refuted. Plan: refine r2c3 with one change each (higher learning rate; twice as many smaller updates at the same number of gradient steps), and retest the cheap global-context trunk at 8 epochs.

### Round 4
Only the mask-layout family has scored above 0 here. The recipe is what moved it. At 2 or 4 PPO epochs it scored about 0. At 8 epochs it reached 0.0146. With twice as many smaller updates (64 envs, r3c2) it reached 0.038, though the seeds varied widely (0.066 and 0.010). A learning rate of 2e-3 (0.0205) and the global-context trunk (0.0195) each scored a little above their 0.0146 baseline, which is within seed noise but in the right direction. Training success is still low (about 0.01 to 0.02), so the agent looks undertrained and sample-limited, not overfitted. Updating more often per sample is the clearest trend so far. This is the last round, so I will exploit: three single changes to r3c2. (1) Halve the rollout again, for about 120 updates. (2) Use lr 2e-3. (3) Add the global-context trunk.

## Trial it ended with
name: Global-context trunk on r3c2 recipe
hypothesis: Uses r3c3's global-board-context bias inside the residual block, trained on r3c2's 61-update recipe. On the 30-update recipe, global context scored 0.0195 against 0.0146, and both of its seeds were above 0.01. Knowing the board-wide progress should help with build order and with stopping at the right time, at almost no extra FLOPs. Expect dev above 0.038. Refuted if dev is at or below 0.038.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: The text never names a column shift or a wraparound offset. Round 1 only guesses that "each world's actions or footprints may be arranged differently" and tests rotations and flips (dihedral layouts), which is the wrong kind of change. Round 2 mentions "where the brick lands under its footprint" and pooling "without assuming its shape or anchor corner", but treats this as a limit on the agent's precision, not as a landing offset. Later rounds blame training recipes and limited samples.
